The Siege of Turin is remembered as the culmination of Eugene of Savoy's war of maneuver in 1705 and 1706, universally regarded by military historians as an operational masterpiece of early modern warfare.
On the morning of September 7, the besiegers woke to find Prince Eugene of Savoy had marched 250 miles across Italy to trap them inside their own trench lines.
Hanging in the balance was the control of southern Europe. For King Louis XIV, victory meant uncontested dominance; defeat meant a destroyed army and an empty treasury. For Eugene, it was the culmination of a twenty-year vendetta. He would risk his life fighting in the front lines, determined to achieve victory at any cost and break the monarch who had once exiled him.
